1:
The vision is granted on all hands to be obscure, and the readings divide between a scheme of empires and a general doctrine of providence. Calvin surveys what others have made of it. Those who find the four Gospels in the four chariots give a very frigid view, and he warns against futile refinements which of themselves vanish away: allegories delight many, but we ought reverently and soberly to interpret the prophetic writings, and not to fly in the clouds, but ever to fix our foot on solid ground. Others take the chariots for the changes in Chaldea and Assyria, Nineveh overthrown that Babylon might be the seat of empire, then the Persian, then the Macedonian, and last the Roman, whose horses are of different colours because some of the Caesars raged cruelly and some showed more lenity. Calvin thinks it simpler that the chariots signify the changes which happened not in Chaldea only but in Judea and among other nations, since the fourth wandered almost through the whole world.

Clarke keeps the imperial scheme and matches it to an earlier vision of horns: red for the Chaldeans who overthrew the Assyrians, black for the Persians founded by Cyrus, white for the Greeks under Alexander, and the party-coloured for the Romans, or for the divided Greeks, the Lagidae who subdued Egypt and the Seleucidae who took Syria. Henry rehearses the same scheme, the red passing unmentioned afterwards because that monarchy was now extinct and the bay taken by some for the Goths and Vandals; but he confesses himself very much in the dark, and inclines rather to read the vision of providence generally. Wesley takes the chariots for angels, who are sometimes styled the chariots of God.

The mountains of brass are read almost alike by all. Calvin takes them for God's hidden counsel, decreed before the creation of the world, so that things before they break forth into action lie inclosed as between narrow passes; the poets call fate unavoidable, but that sentiment is profane, and the brass tells against those who make God foreknow conditionally, as though events depended on the free will of men. Henry puts it as an image: we could as soon grasp the mountains in our arms as comprehend the divine counsels in our finite understandings, and as soon remove mountains of brass as alter any of God's purposes. Clarke calls them the strong barriers of God's purposes, restraining those powers within the times and limits appointed, and Wesley the immoveable decrees. Ellicott alone looks for real hills behind the vision, finding the prototypes in the Mount of Olives and Mount Zion, between which lies the Valley of Jehoshaphat, a name that means the Lord judges; but he holds the mountains themselves visionary.

On the colours Gill offers three readings at once, of ministers, of angels, or of monarchies, and under the last takes the red for the Chaldeans, whose soldiers were clothed in red and whose chariots were like flaming torches. Of the white he notes that such horses were used in triumphs in token of victory, were reckoned the swiftest, and were counted a good omen in dreams. Keil and Delitzsch reads the colours as fixed emblems of judgment: red the colour of blood points to war, black the colour of grief to dearness and famine, and the speckled to pestilence, so that the three great judgments are set out together. Wesley agrees in substance and adds that the mixed colour signifies a mixt state of affairs.

Ellicott presses the wording twice. Red is applicable to cows but bay to horses, and he would render the first colour so. In the fourth chariot he would read only the first word, grey, following the Syriac by conjecture, since as the Hebrew stands the grisled and the bay are identical here while afterwards distinguished, and the red are never mentioned again.
4:
The angel's answer names the four as spirits of the heavens, and the voices divide over the word. Clarke takes them simply as ministers of God's wrath against the sinful nations of the world. Wesley makes them angels who reside in heaven till employed, go thence when employed, and having done their work return thither, standing meanwhile as servants attending their Lord. Ellicott would render the word winds rather than spirits, out of which God makes his messages, as most appropriate here for the working of his Spirit; and he notices a seam where the words of the angel who interprets pass imperceptibly into the prophet's own description of the scene.

The destinations are then matched to history, each voice with his own list. Gill takes the black for the Medes and Persians, and observes that no further mention is made of the red because the kingdom of the Chaldeans was by then extinct. Clarke says the same of the omission and fills out the rest: the black is Cyrus at the head of the Persians and Medes, bringing devastation and death among the Chaldeans, a country always spoken of as the north; the white is Alexander, splendid in his victories and mild towards all that he conquered; the grisled are the Lagidae who founded an empire in Egypt, some good and some bad, some despotic and some moderate, and so party-coloured. Wesley reads the north country as Babylon and the south as Egypt and Arabia, which lay south of Judea, and thinks the grisled managed the Roman power, which was sometimes favourable and sometimes fierce.

Ellicott works from geography rather than from a list of empires. Two chariots go into the north country, he thinks, because there were two powers there to be overcome, the remnant of the old Asshur-Babylonian and the Medo-Persian; and the south country is Egypt, which revolted from Darius after the battle of Marathon, was re-conquered by Xerxes, remained continually in revolt until subdued by Ochos, and was afterwards wrested from Persia by Alexander.

The bay horses that seek leave of their own accord are variously placed. Gill takes them for the Romans, or, since they are distinct from the grisled, for the Huns, Goths and Vandals, who sought to go out of their own places into other countries. Clarke assigns them to the Seleucidae, who conquered Syria and were of unbounded ambition, seeking universal empire, such as Antiochus the Great, though he grants that some think the Romans meant. Wesley reads the seeking as waiting for a commission rather than pressing without one. Ellicott returns to his emendation and holds that once the word rendered red is substituted here and rendered bay, the destinations of all four colours are accounted for.

The closing word about the quieted spirit draws out the sharpest disagreement in the chapter. Clarke reads it as judgment fulfilled upon Assyria and Chaldea, and reports an account making the spotted bay the Roman empire, suited to it because that empire was governed by kings, consuls, dictators and emperors and penetrated southward to Egypt and Africa. Ellicott glosses the crying as summoning and takes spirit in the sense of wrath, so that the phrase means wrath quieted rather than a spirit made to rest. He then denies the whole colour scheme the others build on. Many commentators, he says, have without any warrant drawn their reading of the colours from the Book of Revelation, making red war, black famine, white victory and grisled various chastisements; but they find no reason why famine and victory should be sent especially to the north and chastisements to the south. Better, he thinks, to take the colours as given merely to make the vision distinct. Wesley keeps the plain sense, that the spirit was quieted by the redress of his people's injuries and their bringing back into Canaan.
9:
The chapter turns from vision to sign, and the voices mark the change. Gill notes that the visions being ended the prophetic part of the book begins, the Targum paraphrasing the opening as the word of prophecy from the Lord. Henry draws the contrast more sharply: in the former part God spoke by a vision which only the prophet saw, and here by a sign, or type, which many saw. Keil and Delitzsch adds that the command is not self-explaining, its meaning being given only in the verses that follow.

Who the men from the captivity were is answered differently. Clarke supposes them the persons to whom the silver and golden vessels of the temple were entrusted, who might have had bullion about them for particular purposes, and takes the householder they lodge with for an artificer in silver and gold. Ellicott grants that those who had returned were still called of the captivity, but thinks these were Jews who meant to remain in the land of their exile and were come on a visit to Jerusalem, bringing offerings to show sympathy with the brethren rebuilding. Henry is harder on them: they ought to have bidden a final farewell to Babylon and settled in their own land, and for their remissness thought to atone by this visit. Gill reports the Jewish writers who make the silver and gold a freewill offering sent by their brethren in Babylon, and Wesley reads the errand plainly, to fetch the men if they lodge elsewhere, on the very day they come.

The names raise a difficulty, since two appear altered a few lines later. Ellicott meets it by observing that Heldai is afterwards called Helem and Josiah seems to be called Hen, it being very common for a person to be called by several different names in the Bible, as the father-in-law of Moses is called Hobab, Jethro and Reuel. He adds that the Septuagint declined to treat them as names at all, rendering the three as rulers, their useful men, and those who understood them.

Whether one crown was made or several is disputed from the manuscripts. Clarke reports seven manuscripts collated by two editors, and one ancient copy of his own, with the Syriac and the Chaldee, reading the singular, a crown or tiara; and since Joshua the high priest is alone concerned he thinks one crown only intended. Ellicott reaches nearly the same result by grammar, preferring a composite crown, since the word takes a singular verb afterwards and, though plural in form, seems elsewhere to be used of a single crown or fillet. Henry keeps the plural and makes the metals significant, the silver crown typifying the kingdom of the Messiah while he was on earth and the golden his kingdom in his exalted state, the one as far exceeding the other as gold does silver.

That the crown goes to the priest and not the governor is felt to be the point of the sign. Ellicott refuses an emendation that would add the governor's name beside the priest's: no crown was placed on him, for such an act would have been a seeming restoration of the kingdom when it was not to be restored, the crown having been taken away until he come whose right it is. It was set instead on the head of one who did not properly wear a crown, and for whom this word is never used of the mitre, so that the twofold office of the Messiah, priest and king after the order of Melchizedek, might be symbolised in his person. Henry notices how much tact the act required, since Joshua was far from ambitious of a crown and the people far from wanting a crowned head, and credits the governor's prudence with keeping it from looking like a rival appointment, and God's providence with keeping the kings of Persia from taking umbrage.
12:
Every voice refuses to let the crowned priest be the man meant, and each argues from the same silence. Clarke cannot think the governor is intended, since he is not so much as mentioned; Joshua and his companions are called men of sign, figurative or typical men, so that the crowning and the naming point past them to the Messiah, of whom this priest was the type. He notes that the Chaldee renders the name outright as my Messiah, and takes the growing out of his place for the root and family of David. Ellicott makes the silence do more work: because the governor is not even mentioned, the hearers could not have taken the sign for a bare repetition of the earlier promise, but must have perceived that the temple meant was of a higher nature than the material one then in progress; and he observes that the verb to build is often used figuratively, as of raising up a family. Wesley puts it in a sentence to the priest himself: he is the portrait, the other the Branch itself, and the unseen builder stands beside those building the material house, far inferior to the spiritual temple. Gill notes only that the promise is repeated for confirmation.

On the priest seated upon a throne they agree in substance, differing in emphasis. Clarke presses the doubling: he shall bear the glory and have all the honour of it, for none can do this but himself, and being both a royal king and a royal priest he offers the only available atonement. Ellicott finds the pronoun most emphatic in both clauses, implying that he shall be the true builder and he the true ruler, and defends the plain rendering. Priest cannot be softened into prince, since the earlier mention of the high priest limits its meaning; and throne cannot be reduced to a seat, since the regal dignity of the Branch was already recognised from the older prophets. Wesley adds that the glory of both crowns abides on him, and that sitting speaks at once of royal magnificence and its perpetuity.

The counsel of peace between them both is the hardest clause here, and Ellicott canvasses four readings before his own. That the two are the Messiah and some ideal priest he rejects, since he cannot see how such a thought could have occurred to the hearers, and since there is no special reason to speak of unity between a king and a priest, the two having seldom been at variance in history, though prophets and kings were. That the two are the offices of priest and king he rejects because a counsel of peace cannot exist between two abstracts. That they are the two characters combined in one person he rejects as making the clause superfluous, since there is no need to assert unity between characters already united. The last, that the clause describes a plan devised by the Messiah in his double character, he rejects as agreeing with the thought of neither Testament. The phrase can only mean between two persons, and the only two mentioned are the Branch and the Lord himself; he admits it would have been easier had the text run between him and the Lord, and grants that to the original hearers it must have sounded enigmatical. He records that the Greek turns it differently again, setting a priest at the right hand and a peaceful council between the two.

The others reach their terms by shorter roads. Clarke reasons from the same silence, that the two cannot be the governor and the priest, and puts the peace between heaven and earth between the Father and the Son. Wesley holds the very reading Ellicott dismisses as abstract, that the peace made for God's people rests on the two offices, the priestly making their peace with God and the kingly delivering them from their spiritual enemies.
14:
The crowns are given a destination, and the voices disagree about what they are to commemorate. Clarke reports that one of his own manuscripts has the plural corrected into the singular, and that the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Arabic read one crown, while the Chaldee turns the clause differently again and makes it praise rather than crowns; the sense, he thinks, is that the crown made for Joshua was to be delivered to the men named and laid up in the temple as a memorial of this typical transaction. Ellicott also prefers the singular, since the verb here is singular, and takes the memorial to be of the donors' piety. Wesley keeps the two crowns and takes the memorial to be of the Messiah's certain and speedy coming, remarking of the men themselves that we know no more of them than their names. Gill notes only that the first of them is the same person under a second name.

Who the far off are is answered almost alike, and Gill is at most pains to say what they are far off from. It is not the material temple that is meant, he holds, nor is this a prophecy fulfilled when a stranger repaired that house, as one Jewish commentator suggests, but the spiritual temple, the church; and the calling of the Gentiles is the thing foretold. They are afar off from God, in not having his image upon them, in subjection to his law, in the knowledge and fear of him, and in communion with him; afar off from Christ, in the knowledge of his person and righteousness, in love to him and faith in him; and afar off from the Spirit, from the people of God, and from any solid hope of eternal life. Clarke says the same more briefly, that the Gentiles shall come and become part of the new temple as living stones. Ellicott is careful not to narrow it, taking the far off for hardly the Jews of the Dispersion only but for non-Jews also, and rendering the next words as working at the building rather than building in it. Wesley allows the verse a double reference at once, one to the Jews and the material house, the other to the bringing in of the Gentiles.

The last clause divides them again, and here Ellicott makes the most drastic proposal in the chapter. He holds the received rendering inadmissible, though it has the support of two Jewish commentators, and he will not treat the sentence as breaking off deliberately, since the hearers could never have filled up the gap for themselves. It only remains, he concludes, to suppose that the rest of the passage has been lost, and he grants that no tradition survives to that effect. Clarke takes the words as they stand and reads them as a proof offered in advance: the predictions concerning the twofold office would be so circumstantially fulfilled that the hearers would be obliged to acknowledge the messenger's commission, and the rebuilding of their own house would follow upon their obedience. Wesley divides the promise into a literal part, to be fulfilled in their own day on that condition, and a mystical part, in which the Gentiles come in as brethren and help to build the spiritual temple.
